sample.NAME: Big Bend Seagrasses
sample.PRESERVE_DESCRIPTION_SUMMARY:
The Big Bend Seagrasses Aquatic Preserve, established in 1985, covers over 984,000 acres of Florida’s Gulf Coast along the Big Bend Region, making it the largest of the aquatic preserves. Located within Florida’s “Nature Coast”, the Big Bend Seagrasses Aquatic Preserve is considered to be one of the most pristine coastal areas in all of Florida. The preserve encompasses a large complex of estuaries and bays and includes large stretches of coastline that remain largely undeveloped, being described as one of the least polluted coastal regions in the continental United States. This portion of the coast is unique in that it is an extensive area with no offshore barrier islands, where a number of rivers, creeks, and marshes discharge directly into the Gulf of Mexico. 
Aptly named, the Big Bend Seagrasses Aquatic Preserve is primarily composed of extensive seagrass beds and saltwater marshes. These areas are extremely productive and biologically rich, with nearly 2,000 native species documented within, including more than 800 species of plants and more than 1,000 species of animals. The dense seagrasses and extensive salt marshes found here support a wide variety of species, many of which are commercially and recreationally important or of special concern. The extensive area of this preserve supports a wide range of recreational activities and intersects multiple state parks and wildlife management areas. Visitors often engage in fishing, boating, kayaking, and wildlife watching, all of which offer excellent opportunities to observe and appreciate the untouched scenic beauty and diversity of wildlife found within.
sample.SHORT_DESCRIPTION_SUMMARY: Big Bend Seagrasses Aquatic Preserve is located on Florida's Gulf Coast and spans over 150 miles of coastline, extending from Apalachee Bay southward to the Withlacoochee River. The main communities located along the coastline of the aquatic preserve include Keaton Beach, Steinhatchee, Horseshoe Beach, Suwannee and Cedar Key.

sample.NAME: Tomoka Marsh
sample.PRESERVE_DESCRIPTION_SUMMARY:
The Tomoka Marsh Aquatic Preserve, established in 1969, covers 2,800 acres of Florida’s East Coast, between Ormond Beach and Flagler Beach. The preserve is an estuarine system composed of five distinct areas that include portions of the Halifax River, Smith Creek, Bulow Creek, the Tomoka River, and the Tomoka Basin, and has two Atlantic Ocean connections via the Halifax River: the Ponce DeLeon Inlet, 24 miles to the south, and Matanzas Inlet, approximately 28 miles to the north.
The aquatic preserve supports a number of community types but is most notably characterized by the extensive salt marsh, which provides habitat for a wide range of animals, including birds, mammals, reptiles, insects, fish, and shellfish. More than 175 bird species have been observed within the preserve, foraging and nesting within the marsh. The Halifax Islands, a 12-island archipelago created by the dredging of the river in the 1930s, have also become important bird habitats and serve as rookery sites for a number of species. Several listed species can also be found within the preserve, including the Florida manatee. The waters of the Halifax River serve as an important summer refuge for these animals, leading to the establishment of the Halifax and Tomoka Rivers Manatee Refuge in 2003, to better enhance their protection.
For over a hundred years, visitors and residents have enjoyed the extraordinary views of open water and vibrant birdlife provided by the Tomoka River and its extensive natural communities. Today, visitors to the preserve enjoy a variety of recreational activities, including fishing, kayaking, canoeing, boating, and nature watching, all of which offer excellent opportunities to explore the unique wildlife and scenic beauty of this remarkable estuarine area.
sample.SHORT_DESCRIPTION_SUMMARY: Tomoka Marsh Aquatic Preserve is situated on the northeast coast of Florida. It is positioned along the Tomoka River and portions of the Halifax River. The preserve sits between the towns of Ormond Beach and Flagler Beach.

sample.NAME: Mosquito Lagoon
sample.PRESERVE_DESCRIPTION_SUMMARY:
The Mosquito Lagoon Aquatic Preserve, established in 1970, is a 3,500-acre expanse of the Indian River Lagoon in southern Volusia County. Unique among the inland waters of Florida’s Atlantic coast, the preserve offers visitors a feeling of isolation and wilderness, despite its relatively short distance from homes and development. Full of maze-like waterways, winding channels, and spoil islands, Mosquito Lagoon’s distinctive landscape can be attributed to dragline ditches, dug in the 1940s to control mosquito populations. 
Oyster reefs, seagrass beds, and mangrove forests dominate this unique lagoonal ecosystem, which supports a wide diversity of marine life. Salinity levels in the lagoon are comparable to that of the ocean, and several species of sea fish regularly spawn within. The lagoon hosts a resident population of bottlenose dolphins and provides habitat for nine federally protected species. Commercially important to the region, the lagoon supports a multi-million-dollar fishing industry. Visitors to the preserve often enjoy fishing and boating while exploring the many winding waterways of this uniquely wild ecosystem.
sample.SHORT_DESCRIPTION_SUMMARY: Mosquito Lagoon Aquatic Preserve is in east-central Florida in southern Volusia County south of Ponce de Leon Inlet. It is adjacent to two incorporated municipalities — New Smyrna Beach and Edgewater — and 50 miles northeast of Orlando. It is bounded on the west by the Florida mainland and on the east by a chain of barrier islands.

sample.CSO: The Friends of St. Joseph Bay Preserves, Inc.
sample.NAME: St. Joseph Bay State Buffer Preserve
sample.PRESERVE_D:
The St. Joseph Bay State Buffer Preserve is located in Port. St. Joe, Florida. St. Joseph Bay State Buffer Preserve provides an essential buffer to St. Joseph Bay Aquatic Preserve that helps protect the bay's water quality, natural productivity and critical habitats.

The dune/swale system formed by sand dunes in St. Joseph Bay State Buffer Preserve, created during ancient changes in sea level, is one of the most stable and clearly defined of such topographic features found anywhere. The buffer preserve also includes Money Bayou - an unusual tidal creek that flows directly into the Gulf of America instead of an intervening bay or sound.

St. Joseph Preserve State Buffer Preserve protects an intact natural coastal landscape with one of the highest concentrations of rare plants in the southeastern United States, including globally imperiled species such as Chapman's rhododendron (Rhododendron chapmannii), Telephus spurge (Euphorbia telephioides) and pinewoods aster (Aster spinulosus).

This feature class shows the boundary of the St. Joseph Bay State Buffer Preserve as of June 2025.
